reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: The classic nodular type is a slow-growing, pearly or translucent papule with rolled edges, surface telangiectasia, and sometimes central ulceration (the rodent ulcer)
It is the most common human cancer and arises chiefly on chronically sun-exposed skin, especially the head and neck
Recognise the main subtypes: nodular, superficial (often a scaly erythematous patch on the trunk), morphoeic/infiltrative (a scar-like indurated plaque with ill-defined margins), and pigmented
Dermoscopy showing arborising vessels, blue-grey ovoid nests, and leaf-like areas supports the diagnosis
Although BCC almost never metastasises, it is locally invasive and can cause substantial tissue destruction if neglected, particularly around the eyes, nose, and ears

Treatment is guided by subtype, size, site, and risk, ranging from surgical excision (with margin-controlled surgery for high-risk facial lesions) to topical or destructive therapies for low-risk superficial disease
Multiple or early-onset BCCs should prompt consideration of predisposing conditions such as basal cell naevus (Gorlin) syndrome or prior radiation exposure
Advise lifelong photoprotection and skin surveillance, as a diagnosis of BCC predicts further skin cancers
reference.pathophysiology: Basal cell carcinoma is a malignancy of the basal keratinocytes of the epidermis and follicular structures, driven predominantly by ultraviolet-induced DNA damage. Aberrant activation of the Hedgehog signalling pathway, commonly through inactivating mutations in the PTCH1 tumour-suppressor gene or activating changes in SMO, is central to tumour development, alongside UV signature mutations in TP53. The tumour grows as nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and a surrounding fibromyxoid stroma. Its behaviour is locally invasive rather than metastatic, and infiltrative or morphoeic patterns spread with subclinical extension that explains higher recurrence when margins are inadequate.
additionalDifferentials: Amelanotic or pigmented melanoma (for a pigmented BCC)
Intradermal or other benign melanocytic naevus
Bowen's disease or a plaque of psoriasis or eczema (for superficial BCC)
additionalInvestigations: Diagnostic skin biopsy to confirm the diagnosis and define the histological subtype, which guides treatment
Dermoscopy as an adjunct to clinical assessment
Full skin examination for synchronous skin cancers
Imaging in advanced or deeply infiltrative disease to assess local extension
Consideration of genetic assessment when multiple lesions occur at a young age
redFlags: A non-healing, ulcerating, or bleeding lesion on sun-exposed skin, which is a hallmark of malignancy
An ill-defined, indurated, scar-like plaque suggesting an infiltrative or morphoeic tumour with deep spread
Lesions at high-risk facial sites (eyes, nose, ears) where local destruction threatens vital structures
Numerous or early-onset tumours suggesting an inherited cancer syndrome or prior radiotherapy
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent because metastasis is exceedingly rare, and appropriately treated tumours are usually cured; however, incompletely excised or high-risk subtypes recur and can cause significant local morbidity, and patients remain at higher lifetime risk of further skin cancers requiring ongoing surveillance.
pitfalls: Mistaking a morphoeic BCC for a scar and underestimating its true extent
Treating a superficial BCC as eczema or psoriasis and delaying diagnosis
Choosing a non-surgical or narrow-margin approach for high-risk or recurrent facial tumours
Failing to arrange ongoing skin surveillance after a first diagnosis
management: Surgical excision with predetermined margins as first-line treatment for most tumours
Margin-controlled Mohs micrographic surgery for high-risk, recurrent or facial lesions with subclinical spread
Topical imiquimod or fluorouracil, or destructive techniques such as cryotherapy or curettage and cautery, for low-risk superficial disease
Radiotherapy for patients unsuitable for surgery or as an adjuvant
Hedgehog pathway inhibitors such as vismodegib or sonidegib for locally advanced or metastatic disease
Lifelong skin surveillance for local recurrence and new primary skin cancers
Multidisciplinary team input for advanced or complex tumours
